title: Track without scoring yourself
summary: Follow what moves, without turning your notes into a report card.

why.title: Why observing changes something
why.paragraph1: Recording where you stand is not administrative busywork. A meta-analysis covering many experiments showed that monitoring progress toward a goal increases, on average, the chances of reaching it.
why.paragraph2: The effect was clearer when monitoring was made explicit—written down or shared—rather than kept in mind.
why.paragraph3: Observation also works outside of measurement: it brings attention back to a behavior that had become automatic, which is sometimes enough to open up a choice.
why.keyPoint1: Write your observation rather than keeping it in your head.
why.keyPoint2: Aim for regular rather than exhaustive tracking.
why.keyPoint3: Observing is already an action, not a preparation.

what.title: What to record, and what not to
what.paragraph1: Useful information is general: a time, a place, a state, a strategy you tried, how you felt afterwards. That is enough for a pattern to appear.
what.paragraph2: Explicit details, on the other hand, add nothing to the analysis and create extra risk if your device is lost or seen by someone else.
what.paragraph3: A good test before writing: would this note help me decide something next week? If the answer is no, it can stay unwritten.

noScore.title: An observation, not a grade
noScore.paragraph1: The same data can be read two ways: “three events this week” is information; “I failed, three times” is a verdict. Only the first lets you adjust anything.
noScore.paragraph2: A meta-regression of healthy-eating and physical-activity interventions found that self-monitoring was the single most decisive technique, and that combining it with other self-regulation techniques—setting a goal, comparing, adjusting—outperformed the other interventions.
noScore.paragraph3: That is also why StopCorn assigns no moral score and no streak whose loss erases everything you have done.
noScore.keyPoint1: Describe the facts, leave the verdict aside.
noScore.keyPoint2: Compare with your starting point, not with an ideal.
noScore.keyPoint3: Data is there to help you decide, not to judge you.

gaps.title: Gaps in the data
gaps.paragraph1: There will be days without notes. That is normal, and it does not make the rest unusable.
gaps.paragraph2: Missing data is not the same as no events, though: when you read a trend, keep in mind what was never recorded before drawing a conclusion.
gaps.paragraph3: Picking tracking back up after a break is worth more than a perfect history. Monitoring does not have to be complete to be useful.

rhythm.title: A review rhythm
rhythm.paragraph1: Notes become meaningful when you reread them. A short, regular appointment—for example, ten minutes once a week—can be a starting point.
rhythm.paragraph2: Look at three things: what recurs, what helped, and what you want to adjust next. To begin with, choosing a single adjustment can make its effects easier to read.
rhythm.paragraph3: If the review turns into self-reproach, try reframing the questions: what keeps recurring, what helped, and what do you want to test next?
rhythm.keyPoint1: Set a short review on a fixed day.

reflectionPrompt: Which day of the week could you set aside for a short review of your notes?
